question: Who are the people described as seeing it?

positions.position: People generally, when confronted with the Resurrection or Hereafter.
positions.reasons: Muqatil, Qatada as transmitted by Abd al-Razzaq and al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others describe people without restricting the group. Ibn Kathir places the perception after they rise from their graves.

positions.position: The disbelievers, specifically the Meccan or Quraysh unbelievers in some accounts.
positions.reasons: Al-Tabari calls them deniers; al-Wahidi al-Basit and Ibn al-Jawzi identify Quraysh, as does al-Baghawi; Bursevi particularly names Meccan unbelievers. Al-Biqai says disbelievers give differing estimates of their stay.

turns_on: Whether the verse's general plural is read as humanity at resurrection or as the deniers addressed by the closing warning.

question: What do they see?

positions.position: The Hour, Resurrection, or the reality of the Hereafter that had been promised.
positions.reasons: Muqatil and al-Tabari say the Hour; al-Wahidi al-Basit says what they denied; al-Razi says what was promised. Ibn Kathir places the sight after rising from the graves; al-Tusi's reported Qatada wording speaks of the affair of the Hereafter.

question: Which stay will seem brief?

positions.position: Their earthly life.
positions.reasons: Qatada, reported by Abd al-Razzaq, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Suyuti, says the worldly life shrinks when the Hereafter is seen. Al-Mawardi cites 10:45; al-Wahidi al-Basit and al-Razi invoke 46:35. Al-Tabatabai cites 23:114 while rejecting this as the intended sojourn. Alusi allows this for some people.

positions.position: Their time in the graves, or the interval from death to resurrection.
positions.reasons: Al-Wahidi al-Wajiz attributes their underestimation to the terror of resurrection. Al-Qurtubi reports this from some exegetes. Study Quran calls it the view of most commentators and cites 10:45, 17:52, 20:103–104, 23:112–114, 30:55 and 46:35. Al-Tabatabai prefers it because all earthly life is counted for judgment; Alusi allows it for others. Some sources present world and grave as alternatives, while al-Biqai mentions both together.

positions.position: The interval from asking about, or being warned of, the Hour until its arrival.
positions.reasons: Al-Tabatabai reports and rejects the interval from asking: people witness the span only at resurrection, and death rather than their question precedes that sight. Alusi prefers understanding a short stay after the warning or threat; the context of the impatient challenge supports it.

turns_on: The antecedent of the implied stay: earthly life, the grave period, or the time since the question and warning; al-Tabatabai tests this against what is witnessed at resurrection and what immediately precedes it.

question: How long does their stay seem to have lasted?

positions.position: Only one end or part of a day, an evening or morning, less than a complete day.
positions.reasons: Muqatil describes afternoon to sunset or morning until the sun rises higher; al-Tabari calls them the first and last parts of a day. Al-Kashshaf, Ibn Atiyya, al-Nasafi, al-Biqai and others stress less than a whole day. Al-Qummi, reported by al-Tabatabai, also says part of a day; al-Qurtubi relates the short stay to 10:45.

positions.position: As little as an hour or moment.
positions.reasons: Al-Wahidi al-Basit and al-Razi compare 46:35. Al-Biqai recalls the judgment scene in 10:45 where people say an hour, alongside reports of a day or part of one; he says differing estimates express the same brevity beside the endless future.

positions.position: One whole day.
positions.reasons: Al-Qurtubi transmits this from al-Dahhak on Ibn Abbas. Al-Biqai links an answer of a day or part of one to the question about years in 23:112–113.

turns_on: Whether the stated evening or morning remains a fraction of one day or is expressed in related reports as an hour or a day.

question: What time does ʿashiyyah denote here?

positions.position: The later part of the day, from noon or afternoon until sunset.
positions.reasons: Muqatil gives afternoon to sunset; Ibn Abbas as transmitted by Ibn Kathir defines it from noon to sunset. Al-Tabari and al-Farra treat it as the day's final end; al-Qurtubi calls it afternoon. Sībawayh reports al-Khalil's plural ʿashiyāt/ʿashiyānāt for successive portions of an evening, each reckoned an ʿashiyyah.

question: What does ḍuḥā mean in this phrase?

positions.position: The day's bright morning or forenoon, from sunrise until noon in explicit definitions.
positions.reasons: Muqatil says morning until the sun rises higher; Ibn Abbas as transmitted by Ibn Kathir and Bursevi define sunrise to noon. Bint al-Shati cites Quranic uses opposite evening, the bringing forth of sunlight at 79:29, and appointed event time at 7:98 and 20:59; these oppose taking it as the whole day. Al-Damghani defines ḍuḥā as the sunlit beginning of the day, opposed here to evening. Ibn al-Jawzi derives it from visibility and the spread of sunlight, adducing ordinary uses for open exposure, sacrifice at forenoon, bright nights, and prominent outskirts; he and reported exegetes identify 79:46 as a forenoon use, also citing 20:59 and 93:1.

positions.position: The early or dawn side of the day.
positions.reasons: Al-Wahidi al-Wajiz and al-Baghawi describe the early morning or dawn; Ibn al-Jawzi calls it the first part. Al-Farra's Arabic pairing makes it the beginning opposed to evening's end.

positions.position: It can stand metaphorically for the whole day.
positions.reasons: Al-Tibi, reported by Alusi, allows evening or forenoon to stand for the day; the added pronoun reinforces it, like saying one saw with one's own eyes. Alusi allows the pronoun to reinforce this reading too. Bint al-Shati weighs against it from Quranic usage. Al-Zarkashi says the short forenoon can stand for the whole day.

positions.position: The morning represents worldly life when people see the Hereafter.
positions.reasons: Study Quran reports this from some commentators and mentions 93:1.

turns_on: Whether ḍuḥā names a bounded morning period, extends to the whole day, or symbolizes worldly life; Bint al-Shati appeals to other Quranic uses.

question: How does 'or its forenoon' attach the morning to the evening?

positions.position: The suffix refers to the evening by an expansive attachment: its forenoon is the morning of the same day.
positions.reasons: Al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Jawzi identify the final alif and ha as referring to ʿashiyyah; al-Tabrisi, al-Razi's grammarians, al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi and others license the attachment because both periods belong to one day, though morning ordinarily precedes evening. Al-Samin calls it figurative and notes the cadence. Al-Farra's example from a Banu Uqayl poet uses ʿashiyyat al-hilal for the new moon's setting or hidden phase; al-Thaʿlabi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi repeat it. Ibn Atiyya cites brevity; Abu Hayyan calls the idafa expansive. Ibn ʿAbd al-Salam, as reported by al-Zarkashi, says relating the forenoon to the evening's day makes the spans comparable: a long day's forenoon could otherwise equal a short day's evening.

positions.position: The expression can pair an evening with its following morning, as Arabic pairs the ends of adjacent periods.
positions.reasons: Al-Farra allows an evening with the next morning or a morning with its previous evening. Al-Zajjaj distinguishes 'morning and its evening' of the same day from 'evening and its morning' of the following day. Al-Wahidi and al-Razi report al-Farra and al-Zajjaj's day association while also citing the next-morning idiom; Ibn al-Jawzi transmits al-Farra's paired-end explanation. Al-Kashshaf as reported by Alusi says the possessive wording rules out a stretch from one day's evening to another day's forenoon.

positions.position: The final alif and ha are grammatical additions, so the sense is simply 'an evening or a morning'.
positions.reasons: Ata from Ibn Abbas, reported by al-Wahidi al-Basit and al-Razi, treats the ending as additive rather than a time relation.

positions.position: The suffix reinforces a metaphor in which either end stands for the entire day.
positions.reasons: Al-Tibi, reported by Alusi, compares the emphasis to 'I saw with my own eyes.' Alusi allows this reinforcement, though he prefers the less forced ordinary attachment.

positions.position: The suffix refers to the day implied by the evening, since an evening itself has no morning.
positions.reasons: Al-Suyuti explicitly assigns the pronoun to the implied day. Al-Zarkashi also identifies it as that same day's forenoon.

turns_on: Whether the suffix has a same-day antecedent, licenses an adjacent morning, is merely additive, or reinforces a whole-day metaphor; the Quranic phrasing and Arabic idiom are invoked.

question: Why is their past stay perceived as so brief?

positions.position: Seeing the Hereafter or Resurrection makes worldly duration shrink in retrospect.
positions.reasons: Qatada's formulation appears through Abd al-Razzaq, al-Tabari, al-Tabrisi, Ibn Kathir and al-Suyuti. Al-Mawardi compares 10:45; al-Wahidi al-Basit 46:35. Al-Biqai contrasts the moment with endless future and cites the Prophet's image of a finger dipped in the sea.

positions.position: The terror of what they see makes the grave or worldly stay seem short.
positions.reasons: Al-Wahidi al-Wajiz expressly attributes underestimation to terror; al-Qurtubi's reported grave view does likewise. Al-Nasafi and Jishumi stress the Resurrection's overwhelming condition and terrors.

positions.position: Past time feels short because it is finished, while an uncertain future draws attention and anxiety.
positions.reasons: Kur'an Yolu gives this psychological explanation.

positions.position: Earthly time is illusory and loses meaning in the ultimate reality of the Hereafter.
positions.reasons: Asad cites 2:259, 17:52, 18:19, 20:103, 23:112 and 30:55 for this conception.

turns_on: The notes variously ground the perceived compression in encounter with the Hereafter, terror, ordinary perception of the past, or the nature of earthly time.

question: What lesson does the brief comparison convey?

positions.position: Worldly pleasures and life pass quickly, so the warning calls for preparation.
positions.reasons: Al-Nahhas warns that worldly people soon leave pleasures. Elmalili says the cautious escape the Hour's terrors while the heedless meet lasting calamity; Kur'an Yolu contrasts short life with everlasting afterlife.

positions.position: The Hour is near or should not be dismissed as distant.
positions.reasons: Abu Hayyan says the comparison brings the Hour close. Islahi says judgment will make the worldly stay seem only an evening or morning, so delay is no ground for dismissing it; Alusi connects this to the challengers' impatient question.

positions.position: The Resurrection is tremendous and terrifying.
positions.reasons: Jishumi says these verses demonstrate its great condition and many terrors; al-Wahidi al-Wajiz and al-Nasafi say its terror makes the stay seem short.

turns_on: The authors draw different lessons from the same perceived brevity: worldly transience, imminent judgment, or the gravity of Resurrection.

question: How does this comparison relate to other Quranic statements about time at judgment?

positions.position: It echoes statements that people will reckon their past as an hour, a day, or part of one.
positions.reasons: Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi cite 10:45; al-Wahidi al-Basit, al-Baghawi, al-Kashshaf, al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi invoke 46:35. Al-Biqai quotes the judgment scene of an hour and connects the day-or-part-day reply to 23:112–113. Study Quran lists 10:45, 17:52, 20:103–104, 23:112–114, 30:55 and 46:35; Asad cites 2:259, 17:52, 18:19, 20:103, 23:112 and 30:55. Al-Tabatabai cites 23:114 while disputing an earthly-life referent.

question: How does this closing comparison answer the earlier question about the Hour?

positions.position: It confirms the warning: the Hour will arrive swiftly and the Prophet's task is warning, while God knows its time.
positions.reasons: Alusi prefers a short stay after the warning or threat and says the sentence may be circumstantial or independent. Islahi says timing demands should not trouble the Prophet. Alusi rejects construing 79:43 as a substitute for their question or a quotation of it, because 79:44 directly assigns knowledge of the endpoint to God; Ibn Jurayj, reported by al-Suyuti, also glosses that endpoint as God's knowledge.

positions.position: It rebuts disbelievers who mockingly or impatiently demand to know when the Hour will come.
positions.reasons: Alusi ties the rebuke to 79:42 and prefers an interval after the warning. Study Quran says the final verses answer taunts over the Prophet's ignorance of the date.

positions.position: Earlier questions about the Hour ended with revelation assigning its timing to God.
positions.reasons: Aisha reports that the Prophet was repeatedly asked until 79:43–44 came and then stopped asking; al-Hakim authenticated this report. Tariq ibn Shihab instead reports that he often mentioned the Hour, then stopped mentioning it after those verses. Aisha also reports the Prophet telling visiting Bedouins that if their youngest lived a century their own Hour would have come.

turns_on: Whether the preceding question is treated as a request for its unknown date, an impatient taunt, or a warning whose fulfillment will seem near; the reports differ on asking versus mentioning it.

question: What reading or construction is reported for mundhir in the surrounding warning?

positions.position: Several readers use mundhir with tanwin, governing its object.
positions.reasons: Alusi reports Abu Jaʿfar, Shaybah, Khalid al-Hadhdhaʾ, Ibn Hurmuz, Isa, Talha, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Miqsam and Abu Amr through al-Mundhir; he says this is the original construction, while genitive attachment can lighten the expression.

question: How does the verse serve the surah's overall design and transition?

positions.position: It closes the surah's proof of resurrection and human destiny, then returns to the opening and leads into the next surah.
positions.reasons: Al-Biqai says the surah establishes resurrection and gathering after preceding surahs' full exposition, with the oaths bringing the matter to a climax. Its name al-Naziʿat evokes angels extracting souls and the Pharaoh–Moses account; al-Sahirah and al-Tammah also fit the flow. The close returns to the opening through resurrection, then links fear and remembrance to 80:1.

question: What does the passage imply about the experience of the afterlife?

positions.position: The afterlife involves felt experience; a merely spiritual account of comfort or pain is rejected.
positions.reasons: Al-Qurtubi says the passage answers those who claim only spiritual comfort or pain without sensation.

positions.position: Comfort and pain in the afterlife are only spiritual, without sensation.
positions.reasons: Al-Qurtubi identifies and rejects this claim.

turns_on: Whether the verse's account of seeing and sensing the Hour entails sensory experience.

question: What inward meanings are given to the evening and morning?

positions.position: They evoke the setting of truth's light in bodies or its rising from the west; unity makes worldly existence seem imagined.
positions.reasons: Al-Qashani reports this possible inward reading.

positions.position: They signify the bodily and spiritual worlds, passed in two steps before arrival.
positions.reasons: Al-Qashani reports that sensation and intellect conceal these two worlds.

turns_on: Which paired spiritual phases the two short spans symbolize.

question: What recitation virtue is reported for Surat al-Naziʿat?

positions.position: Its reciter will be held in the grave or at resurrection only as long as an obligatory prayer, then enter Paradise.
positions.reasons: Al-Kashshaf reports both grave and resurrection; al-Baydawi reports resurrection and supplies no grading.

question: How are the verses' brief-time expressions used in a reported prayer?

positions.position: A prayer for success invokes the briefness-of-time verses alongside mercy, forgiveness, safety, good deeds, Paradise and rescue from Hell.
positions.reasons: Al-Suyuti transmits the prayer from Anas.

question: How do Arabic temporal nouns such as ʿashiyyah and ḍuḥā behave in context?

positions.position: ʿAshiyyah stays indefinite yet can mean a contextually specified evening; specified ʿashiyyah and ḍuḥā function as accusative time adverbs.
positions.reasons: Sībawayh says ʿashiyyah remains indefinite like ṣabāḥan and masāʾ, though context can identify the day. He explicitly cites this verse for the accusative adverbial use, alongside saḥar, ḍaḥwa, ʿatma, and other time expressions.

positions.position: Some Arabs omit tanwin from ʿashiyyah, by analogy with ghadwa.
positions.reasons: Sībawayh records this usage from some Arabs.

positions.position: Other time expressions vary in definiteness, adverbial use, and context-dependent ellipsis.
positions.reasons: Sībawayh reports Abu ʿAmr on definite ghadwa and bukra, al-Khalil's usage with al-yawm, and Abu al-Khattab's same-day or next-day bukra with 19:62; he also discusses saḥar, event-time answers, omitted kāna in temporal clauses, fixed lā ʿalayka, and dialectal dhā ṣabāḥ.

question: What diminutive and plural forms of the verse's time nouns are attested in Arabic?

positions.position: Time nouns have regular and irregular diminutives, and plural forms can divide a period into successive parts.
positions.reasons: Sībawayh gives ʿashīshiyyah/ʿashiyyān for ʿashiyyah, ḍuḥayyā for ḍuḥā with a verse of al-Nābighah al-Jaʿdī, and other time examples. He explains that diminutives shorten the interval between times, not the time itself; al-Khalil explains aṣīlālā and evening plurals. Sībawayh contrasts personal names and other irregular diminutives.

question: What Arabic hamza substitutions and deletions are described alongside the opening word's hamza?

positions.position: Hamza may be replaced by a matching long vowel or deleted in particular lexical, dialectal, and poetic settings.
positions.reasons: Sībawayh distinguishes replacement before a final hamza and radical from extra-letter hamza, explains lightening after each vowel and poetic meter, and gives dialectal examples including Huthayl, nabī/bariyyah, word-boundary substitution, and deletion amid difficult consonant sequences. These are general Arabic examples; he does not specify a variant of كأنهم.

question: What case and ellipsis patterns occur in Arabic comparisons mentioning ʿashiyyah?

positions.position: After lā, a term may follow syntactic position or the particle's case; poetic lā ka-l-ʿashiyyati examples can imply an omitted verb.
positions.reasons: Sībawayh and al-Khalil explain positional nominative and alternative accusative in lā constructions. Jarir's lā ka-l-ʿashiyyati requires an understood verb because an evening cannot be a visitor; Sībawayh treats kāf as a preposition and cites Dhu al-Rumma, Imruʾ al-Qays, and other comparisons. These examples concern Arabic usage, not this verse's syntax.

question: How can Arabic illā express an exception in the verse's language?

positions.position: An excepted term can be accusative as a corrective 'but' or nominative as an identification with the preceding category.
positions.reasons: Sībawayh contrasts Hijazi accusative with Tamim nominative, citing donkey and verbal-noun examples, al-Khalil's poetic analogy, and examples at 52:28 and 36:43. These establish general uses of illā; he does not assign one of those dialectal constructions specifically to 79:46.

question: What Arabic poetic substitutions and inversions are cited as background for unusual wording?

positions.position: Poets can substitute related names or terms and reverse a relation, sometimes under metrical pressure.
positions.reasons: Ibn Qutayba supplies substitutions of father for son, ancestors for descendants, kinship terms, and poetic reversals in eleven examples. Al-Zarkashi separately cites dual place names for a single place or its surroundings. Neither source explicitly applies these examples to 79:46.

question: What do the accompanying rhetorical notes say about harmony and roughness of wording?

positions.position: Balanced letters can make speech easy and pleasing, while celebrated poetry can contain harsh or obscure passages.
positions.reasons: Al-Rummani and reported al-Khalil distinguish degrees of letter harmony, pronunciation and reception, with the Qur'an placed at the highest level. Al-Baqillani adduces rough passages from Abu Nuwas, al-Aʿsha, Zuhayr and al-Tirmah, then reports a critic's defense of even speech and praise for al-Buhturi and Abu Nuwas. The excerpts make general rhetorical claims, without analyzing this verse's sounds.

question: What general rules of large assimilation are recorded in the recitation notes?

positions.position: Large assimilation merges two moving related letters; Abu ʿAmr is especially associated with it, though transmission manuals differ.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-Jazari defines large and small assimilation, explains proposed names and ease of articulation, cites Abu ʿAmr and poetic Arabic evidence, and records both omission and inclusion by earlier manuals. These notes give no specific assimilated reading of 79:46.

question: What other lexical sense list appears alongside the note on ḍuḥā?

positions.position: The accompanying lexicon also lists seven senses for ḍarar.
positions.reasons: Al-Damghani lists affliction, drought, terrors, illness, decrease, hunger, and harm itself. The list does not gloss ḍuḥā in this verse.

question: What special-property report uses the verse's brief-time expression?

positions.position: A stopped report from Ibn Abbas prescribes writing the verse with 46:35 for difficult childbirth and giving the writing to drink.
positions.reasons: Al-Suyuti transmits the Ibn Abbas report and says his collection presents non-fabricated reports and reports from Companions and Successors that he found concerning Qur'anic special properties.
